full_judgment:
5. The plaintiff-respondent's suit was for declaration of title and confirmation of possession or alternatively khas possession in the land of Schedule 2 to the plaint and for permanent injunction. It is his case that 6 kanis of land of Schedule 1 to the plaint belonged to Abdul Hakim and others in raiyati interest under landlord Badruddoza Chowdhury who obtained a rent decree in RS No. 780 of 1934 against the tenants and in execution thereof in Execution Case No. 721 of 1935 auction purchased the holding for Rs. 25/-. Abdul Hakim and others amicably gave up possession of Schedule 1 land after obtaining remission of balance of decretal dues and being sentenced to jail in a murder case left for Arakan and other places after release. Badruddoza possessed the Schedule 1 land for 2 years then settled by pattas 5 kanis out of 6 kanis land of the holding to proforma-defendant Nos. 21-30, the rest 1 kani being now in possession of his heirs proforma-defendant Nos. 31-34. The plaintiff purchased the suit Schedule 2 land from out of Schedule 1 land from proforma-defendant Nos 21, 22, 28 and 29 by a kabala dated 20-5-58 and is possessing the same. Abdul Hakim's heirs. the defendants, have no title and possession in the suit land. They are threatening the plaintiff with dispossession. Hence the suit. 

 21. Plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession in the suit land and also for permanent injunction. Plaintiffs case, in short, is that, the suit land belonged to Abdul Hakim and others in raiyati interest under landlord Badruddoza Chowdhury predecessors-in-interest of proforma-defendants 31-34 as recorded in RS. khatian. The landlord obtained a decree in Rent Suit No. 780 of 1934 against the tenants and in Rent Execution Case No. 721 of 1935 auction purchased the holding for Rs. 25/- after exempting the balance of the decretal dues as the tenants were unable to pay the balance of Tk.129/- and odd. In such circumstances, the tenants gave up possession amicably in favour of landlord Badaraddoza Chowdhury who held the land for two years in khas possession after merging the raiyati with his Taluki interest. Abdul Hakim and others were entangled in a murder case and they were sentenced to jail and after release from jail they left for Arakan and other places. The landlord settled 5 kanis of lands out of entire 6 kanis of the holding toproforma defendants 21-30 on 26.1.1937 by pattas and the rest one kani is in possession of the heirs of Badaraddoza namely, proforma defendants 31-34. Plaintiff purchased the suitland of Schedule 11 of the plaint out of the land of Schedule I from proforma defendants 21, 22, 28 and 29 by kahala on 30.5. 1958 and is in possession of the same. According to the plaintiff, Abdul Hakim, others and their heirs defendants have no title and possession in the suit land. The positive case of the plaintiff, is that, defendant No. 17, a pleader's clerk who conducted the suit at his instance the defendants threatened the plaintiff with dispossession as defendant No. 17 failed to purchase the land. 

 22. Defendants 1, 3 and 4 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. They contended that the suit land of Schedule 1 of the plaint belonged to their predecessors-in-interest Abdul Hakim and others and that there was never any alleged auction sale of the holding and landlord Badaraddoza never got khas possession in the same. Defendants also assert that the subsequent patta holders namely, defendants 21-30 did not get khas possession in the disputed land and consequently the plaintiff also did not acquire any right, title and interest in the disputed land. The defendants' positive case, is that, they are in possession of the suit land from the time of their predecessors. In the recent settlement operation the suit lands had been recorded in the name and possession of the defendants. It is further asserted in the written statement that Yusuf Ali, proforma defendant No. 30 flied a criminal case being Criminal case No. 374 of 1956 on 13.7.56 under section 447 of the Penal Code against the defendants with the allegation that the defendants dispossessed Yusuf Ali from the suit land and the said criminal case was dismissed for non-prosecution by said Yusuf Ali. 

 25. The learned Munsif disbelieved the plaintiffs case of auction sale of the holding at the instance of landlord Badaraddoza and his khas possession for 2 years and subsequent resettlement by him by pattas to the plaintiffs vendors. The trial Judge also found that the defendants are in continuous possession since the time of their predecessors. Thus, according to the learned Munsif, the suit was barred by limitation as the heirs and successors of the original tenants were in possession for more than 12 years. 

 26. On the contrary, learned lower appellate Court believed the auction sale of the holding by landlord and khas possession by the landlord for two years and subsequent settlement of the suit land to proforma defendant Nos. 21-30, vendors of the plaintiff. The lower appellate Court found title with the plaintiff by virtue of his kabla dated 30.5.1958. The lower appellate Court found that the plaintiffs vendors were in possession and the plaintiff though purchased the suit land in 1958 by kabala, was not in present possession of the disputed land and further found that the defendants were not in continuous possession from the time of their predecessors-in-interest, but they were in possession since 1956 and consequently the suit was not barred by limitation and decreed the suit. 

 30. The learned Munsif disbelieved the auction sale only because the sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession were not produced by the plaintiff in this case. But the lower appellate Court considered the suit Register Ext. 8 and the oral evidence on record and found that the auction sale was for Rs. 25.00 only and after exempting the balance dues, the landlord took amicable possession of the suit land. There is unequivocal statement in the plaint that the tenants took exemption of the balance decretal amount and gave khas possession in favour of the landlord and the landlord took possession thereon. As a matter of fact there is clear averment in the plaint that Badaraddoza after auction purchase got possession in the entire land as far back as 23 years and was in khas possession of the holding of the land by merging the same with the taluki land of the landlord and there was no existence of raiyati land. This was the averment in the plaint and in order to prove khas possession of the landlord evidence was also led that the landlord was in possession for 2 years through one Sarafat Ali. The learned lower appellate Court rightly pointed out that there was no documentary evidence that the landlord took delivery of possession, as sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession were not produced in the case. But the lower appellate Court considered the oral evidence and other attending facts and circumstances in arriving at a finding that the suit register exhibit 8 relates to the suit and the landlord in the circumstances of the present case went into possession amicably after giving exemption of the dues to the tenants. The lower appellate Court considered the evidence of PW 3 Abdul Jabbar admittedly who was a Tahsildar of the Estate of landlord Badaraddoza Chowdhury since 1932 upto War period. This witness testified that the suitland was auctioned purchase by Badaraddoza for Rs. 25.00 after giving exemption to the tenants who gave up possession and the landlord was in possession for 2 years through borgadars. This witness in cross-examination also admitted that when the tenants gave up the land in favour of Badaraddoza he was present and that was 24/25 years back and one Sarafat Ali was the borgadar for 2 years. The lower appellate Court found this witness PW 3 to be a competent witness as he was the Tahsildar of the Estate and defendants' witnesses also admitted that this witness PW 3 was a Tahsilder of the Estate at the relevant time. 

 32. This observation of the trial Court is nothing but a product of surmise and conjecture, as because there is clear statement in the plaint and the plaintiff had adduced oral evidence in support of the khas possession of the landlord, Badaraddoza Chowdhury as indicated above. It is surprising to note that a positive statement in the plaint has been commented by the learned Munsif in such a manner. Further, the trial Court found that. 

 This observation of the trial Court is not correct, as because in the plaint there is clear averment that the suit land was taken in khas possession by the landlord and the same was merged with the Taluki land of the landlord and the landlord was in khas possession. Further the evidence of PW 3 also shows that the landlords were in khas possession for 2 years. The appellate Court further found that there was mentioned in the plaint regarding the khas possession by the landlord and re-settlement thereafter to proforma defendant Nos. 21-30 by pattas Exts. 5-5(c). The appellate Court also considered that in these pattas there are recitals of the rent suit and the execution case as in Exhibit 8 and also clear recitals that the landlord was in khas possession by letting out temporarily. The learned lower appellate Court believed these pattas to be genuine documents and held that those were acted upon. But the trial court disbelieved these pattas as because only proforma defendant No. 30 Yusuf Ali deposed in the case as PW 5. The appellate Court as a Court of fact took a contrary view as taken by the trial Court with respect to these documents. Further, the lower appellate Court also considered Touzi Ext. 3 series and Bakiza Ext. 4 series proved to have been written in the handwriting of landlord Badaroddaza. The appellate Court believed these documents and ultimately found that the plaintiff purchased in 1958 by kabala from the heirs of some of the Pattandars and also from some of pattandars. Further, the appellate Court found that Sarafat Ali was in temporary possession for 2 years under the landlord before he let out these lands to plaintiffs vendor as far back as 24/25 years. The appellate Court also considered Ext. 7 by which one of the pattandars transferred a portion of his patta land by way of Waqf. to a mosque in the locality in the year 1952. The learned lower appellate Court as a court of fact believed these documents and found that plaintiffs vendors had title and possession from whom plaintiff purchased by kabala in 1958. The plaintiff in reality came in picture in 1958 after his purchase. It appears from the evidence of PW 5 Yusuf Ali (proforma defendant No. 30) one of the Pattandars that he brought a criminal case on 13.7.56 being criminal Case No. 374. of 1956 under section 447 of 11e Penal Code against the defendants for dispossessing him. In his testimony PW 5 stated that he did not proceed with the case as defendant No.1 gave up possession in his favour. In the written statement the defendants admitted that the case was not proceeded by proforma defendant No. 30. The lower appellate Court believed this judgment of this criminal case, Exhibit C(2), and the copies of orders in criminal cases Exts. C,C(1). The lower appellate Court as a court of fact considered both the oral and documentary evidences and came to a positive finding that the plaintiffs vendors were in possession of the disputed land and the trouble arose in 1956 when the criminal cases as per Exhibit C(2), and the proceeding under section 107 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Ext. C) was started by defendant No. 31 in 1957. Thus, according to the lower appellate Court, the trouble arose in 1956 when the defendants entered into possession of the same. The trial Court as a court of fact found the defendants to be in continuous possession since the time of their predecessors-in-interest. Whereas the lower appellate Court on consideration of the oral and documentary evidences found that the trouble arose in 1956-57, when the defendants went into possession. This is a factual determination by the lower appellate Court and the appellate Court believed this material aspect regarding possession of the parties. The lower appellate Court also considered the present mutation proceedings, that is, Exhibit C(3) and C(4) dated 6.6.1959 which speaks of the possession of the defendants. Since the lower appellate Court found possession of the defendants from 1956, these mutation proceedings of 1959 were not found to be the basis of continuous possession of the defendants since the time of their predecessors-in-interest. 

 33. A reference to the oral evidence on record will show that the trial Court did not at all speak: a word in the judgment about the defendants' witnesses. It is really surprising that the court of original jurisdiction which was to decide this most vital question of possession of the defendants did not at all consider any of the defendant's witnesses before arriving at the decision that the defendants were in continuous possession since the time of their predecessors-in-interest. In such circumstances, I must refer to the relevant oral evidence on record to see whether the determination of the period of possession by the appellate Court was correct, which was of prime importance in the case. PW 1 Nur Mohammad, the plaintiff came in picture after purchase in 1958 and as such the appellate Court did not give any importance to the testimony of this witness. The material evidence is of PW 3 Abdul Jabbar, a Tahsildar of the Estate whose evidence had already been mentioned earlier in my judgment in extenso. PW 4 Nazir Ahmed, the grand son of one of the proforma-defendants, Yusuf Ali testified that they possessed the land and paid rents. PW 5 Yusuf Ali, (proforma defendant No. 30) testified that they possessed the land for 24/25 years after patta and I defendants never possessed the land. DW 1 Musa Ali, defendant No.3 (present appellant) testified that his father died 20/22 years back and they are in possession of the suit land. DW 2 Badruzzaman was disbelieved by the appellate Court as the evidence of possession given by him was found to be vague by the appellate Court. DW 3 Golam Kader was disbelieved by the lower appellate Court as he had no knowledge as to which lands were possessed by Abdul Hakim and others. The appellate Court found him to be a tutored witness. DW 4 only proved dakhilas, exhibit A series of the defendants. The appellate Court disbelieved these dakhilas as the l origin and genuineness of these dakhilas were very suspicious. DW 5 Sabar Ali was aged about 13 years at the time of deposition and as such both the appellate Court and the High Court Division found that he was not a competent witness to depose about defendants' continuous possession. This being the nature of evidence, the lower appellate Court as a court of fact held that the defendants were not in continuous possession but only entered into possession in 1956-57. Thus, with regard to the evidence on record, the material issue as to the period of possession was correctly determined by the appellate Court Consequently, the suit is not barred 1 by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act Article 142 speaks of recovery of possession of immovable property when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed within 12 years from the institution of the suit. This Article applies only where the plaintiff, while in possession has been dispossessed In the four comers of the plaint no where it has been stated that the plaintiff had been dispossessed. The averment in the plaint is that, the defendants are threatening the plaintiff with dispossession though the defendants have got no right, title and interest in the suit land. There being no assertion of dispossession this suit does not come under Article 142 of the Limitation Act The plaintiff though found to have acquired title was not in present possession and the suit having been filed within 12 years from acquisition of title and the defendants having failed to establish their adverse possession for more than 12 years, this suit cannot be governed by Article 142 of the Limitation Act. The plaintiff having proved his title he is entitled to a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. The present suit really comes within the purview of Article 144 of the Limitation Act. As the suit is governed under Article 144 of the Limitation Act, the plaintiff is entitled to the decree on proof of his title only.
